item.title: Village Planning Board Tackles Water Crisis, Cell Tower Application, and Zoning Reforms
item.description:
The village planning and zoning board addressed a busy agenda this week, grappling with infrastructure challenges, a contentious cell tower proposal, and calls for clearer administrative processes as it pushes forward with comprehensive ordinance reforms.

The meeting opened with public comments expressing community appreciation for the board’s handling of recent village water issues—a concern that has weighed on residents’ minds in recent weeks.

Cell Tower Application Sparks Procedural Debate

A significant portion of the meeting centered on a cell tower application that has raised questions about municipal governance and decision-making authority. The application involves Tyler Carter and Sean Milks as investors, with Nancy Carr as the property owner—a distinction that created confusion over application fees and lease agreements.

Board members expressed frustration over the lack of clear municipal ordinances governing cell tower evaluations. “We need applicable ordinances to form a basis for findings of fact,” one member stated, highlighting the challenge of making objective decisions without localized regulatory standards.

The board emphasized that any approval would require proper ordinances in place and likely would need to proceed through public hearings before final determination.

Subdivision Plan Simplified After Confusion Over State and Local Classifications

The board also discussed a subdivision application that was initially filed by Nancy Carr but subsequently withdrawn. Carr has now proposed a simpler two-lot split plan instead.

The confusion stemmed from misunderstandings between state and village classifications of subdivisions versus lot splits, compounded by issues with plat submissions and premature fee payments. Carr has requested a refund, expressing frustration that she received inadequate explanation about application requirements from the previous administration.

The board tabled the matter pending proper review of documentation and plats, underscoring the importance of meticulous compliance with land use protocols.

Comprehensive Ordinance Reforms on Horizon

Among the board’s unfinished business are 2026 planning and zoning reform ordinances awaiting village council review and public hearings. These reforms aim to modernize the unified fee schedule, application permits, and vacant building policies—all areas identified as needing clarity.

Board members noted that clearer administrative processes could prevent misunderstandings like those experienced by Carr. In smaller municipalities, where staff turnover and limited governance experience can occur, residents need transparent guidance about application requirements and steps.

Water Plant Authority Under Review

The board also discussed the Planning and Zoning Commission’s role concerning village water plant matters. While routine maintenance does not require commission involvement, new construction or significant projects would fall under their jurisdiction, pending legal verification from the village attorney.

The discussion reflects an evolving scope for planning bodies as villages modernize infrastructure and balance traditional land use oversight with utility management.

Other Pending Matters

Additional items on the agenda included:

• Pending liquid waste permits

• Legal proceedings involving property abatement related to an incarcerated resident with a court-appointed guardian ad litem

The meeting concluded with a motion to adjourn.

Next Steps: The village council will review the 2026 planning and zoning ordinance reforms before public hearings are scheduled. Residents interested in these matters are encouraged to monitor village council meeting agendas for updates.

item.title: Alamogordo Residents Struggle with Record PNM Bills as Utility Cites Heat, Staffing Challenges
item.description:
Alamogordo residents are facing unprecedented power bills this summer, with some receiving charges for two months of service in a single statement. The surge has sparked frustration across the community and raised questions about how utility companies handle billing during peak demand periods.

Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) attributed the billing delays to temporary staffing shortages that forced the company to estimate customer bills beginning in July through early August. The utility stated it communicated the situation to customers, local officials, and the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission before implementing estimated billing on July 21.

Residents Face Financial Strain

For many Alamogordo families, the bills have created an unexpected financial burden. One resident described the dilemma facing working-class households across the community.

“Most of us are just minimum wage working class folks and we’re doing our best to just get by? And so bills like this, how are we supposed to pay them and feed our families”? said a local resident in response to high bills.

Another community member highlighted the particular vulnerability of fixed-income households. “For most of the people in Alamogordo, they lived on fixed incomes . So an $600 bill could really put us over the edge and lead to homelessness we live paycheck to paycheck,” he said.

PNM’s Explanation and Response

PNM said the high bills reflect both the estimation process and record energy consumption driven by extreme heat. The utility explained that when actual meter readings aren’t available, its billing system calculates average daily usage from the most recent prior billing period and the same period from the previous year, then applies it to the current cycle.

“We realize that this summer has been extremely hot, and we have seen an unprecedented level of usage on our system. So much as that we’ve hit record peaks multiple times in the last few weeks,” PNM stated.

The company initially apologized for the delayed billing in an email to residents, stating: “We understand that receiving your bill later than expected can be frustrating, and we sincerely apologize for the inconvenience.” The message also noted that PNM is bringing in additional meter readers from other parts of the state and said payment plans may be available for those billed for two months in one billing cycle.

However, residents say the apology doesn’t address their core concern—the actual amount they’re being charged.

Staffing and System Updates

PNM clarified that it did not terminate any meter readers in the Alamogordo area. The company stated it is committed to “finding new opportunities for our meter reader employees as we transition to smart meters on our system.” According to PNM, the empty positions have since been filled, and meter-reading routes in Alamogordo are now fully staffed, with no further missed or delayed reads expected.

Political Response and Calls for Regulation

The billing crisis has drawn attention from political candidates who view it as symptomatic of broader utility and infrastructure challenges across New Mexico. Grace Nagamine, candidate for district 51 state representative, connected the PNM billing surge to larger concerns about utility regulation and aging infrastructure.

“This summer, PNM’s bills hit record highs. Our families are paying more than ever—and higher fuel prices and inflation are making it even worse. Hardworking people are struggling to choose between paying their power bills and paying rent,” Nagamine said.

Nagamine pointed to parallel infrastructure crises, citing recent water system failures in communities like Timberon, where families faced boil-water advisories throughout July. “Local water systems are failing,” Nagamine stated, arguing that communities lack state support to address these challenges.

Nagamine’s platform calls for strengthening the Public Regulation Commission’s authority to mandate rapid compliance for failing utilities, penalize infrastructure neglect, block rate increases during hardship periods, and provide state technical support to local leaders. “When I’m elected, I will draft legislation that gives our communities the support they need,” Nagamine said.

Resources Available to Affected Customers

PNM indicated that several assistance programs are available to struggling customers, including:

• Budget Billing: Smooths out seasonal usage fluctuations across the year

• Good Neighbor Fund: Provides assistance for customers experiencing financial hardship

• Payment Plans: Extend payment due dates for customers who received multi-month bills

• Energy-Saving Programs: Help reduce monthly electricity usage

The utility encouraged residents to visit PNM.com/help to learn more about available options.

Looking Forward

As Alamogordo residents work to resolve their billing issues, the incident has raised broader questions about utility regulation, infrastructure investment, and the ability of local communities to advocate for affordable, reliable service during extreme weather events. State legislators will likely face renewed pressure to address both utility oversight and infrastructure funding in the coming legislative session.

Meanwhile, gigawatts of free energy fall on Alamogordo's sand and rock every day, unused.

item.title: Tularosa School District Strengthens Programs and Approves Bond for Growth
item.description:
Board Approves $1.25M Bond Resolution While Maintaining Stable Tax Rates; New Initiatives Focus on Student Support and Engagement

The Tularosa School District is entering the 2026-27 school year with significant investments in staff, student support, and infrastructure, as the district board approved an amended bond resolution and several student opportunity programs during a recent meeting.

The board unanimously approved an amended resolution correcting the authorization amount for bond issuance to $1.25 million—up from an earlier figure of $1.225 million. The bonds will finance district projects while maintaining existing property tax rates, thanks to a modest increase in assessed valuations across the community.

Expansion Across All Campuses

The district has significantly expanded its workforce, onboarding new staff members across preschool through high school, including additional principals and support personnel. This expansion reflects the district's commitment to leadership development and enhanced educational services as enrollment continues to grow.

"Enrollment remains steady and strong," according to district reports, with 52 students in the preschool program and 161 at Tularosa Elementary School. The district is maintaining approximately 95% attendance, a key metric for funding and program stability that demonstrates strong community engagement.

New Behavioral Support Programs

In response to growing awareness of social-emotional learning needs, the district has introduced innovative behavioral support programs at the elementary school level. New CARE (Connecting and Recovery Environment) rooms and dedicated sensory spaces are designed to assist younger students in managing stress and behavioral challenges in a supportive setting.

"These interventions are critical to student success and reducing classroom disruptions," the district noted, highlighting a progressive approach to early childhood education that extends beyond traditional academics.

Athletics and School Culture

Fall sports programs are fully staffed with strong participation in football and volleyball across middle and high school levels. The programs underscore the district's commitment to extracurricular engagement, which research links to improved academic outcomes and overall student well-being.

At the middle school level, the launch of the Wildcat Claw Citizenship Program and structured house meetings is promoting positive citizenship, leadership, and teamwork among students. These initiatives aim to create a supportive school environment and foster meaningful student engagement.

Recognizing Student Achievement and Community Partnerships

The district is expanding student opportunities through multiple channels. Student artwork created for the "We Bond New Mexico" film project has been recognized, with potential for state and national exhibition opportunities. Additionally, the board approved a Hispanic Multicultural Grant for $6,000 to support Career and Technical Student Organizations (CTSO) extracurricular activities.

The district also authorized student travel to the National FFA Convention in Indianapolis, providing valuable leadership and professional development experiences for students involved in agricultural education programs.

Community Support and Financial Stewardship

The district acknowledged strong community support, including water donations for school events and successful grant awards that enhance educational programs. The board's careful financial planning, including the bond resolution that accommodates district growth without increasing local property tax rates, reflects responsible fiscal stewardship.

"This comprehensive approach—from academic programs and behavior supports to community engagement and fiscal responsibility—places the Tularosa School District in a strong position for continued success," district leadership stated.

The board set the date for the next regular meeting, with remote participation options available for members with scheduling conflicts. All agenda items were approved unanimously.

item.title: A Community Reckons with History: 'First We Bombed New Mexico' Brings Nuclear Justice to Alamogordo
item.description:
The Flickinger Center in Alamogordo filled with an intent, solemn energy on Wednesday evening as residents gathered to witness "First We Bombed New Mexico," Lois Lipman's unflinching documentary about the Trinity nuclear test and its devastating aftermath. But this was far more than a standard film screening. The presence of Congressman Gabe Vasquez and Deb Haaland—the former U.S. Interior Secretary and current Democratic gubernatorial nominee along with in the audience support from Mayor Sharon McDonald, City Commissioner Warren Robinson, candidate for District 51 State Representative Candidate Grace Nagamine and County Commissioner Candidate Evan Lambert Ross—transformed the event into a symbolic moment of political acknowledgment for a community that has waited eight decades for justice.

The timing could not be more significant. Just over a year ago, in July 2025, Congress finally expanded the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) to include New Mexico's long-excluded Downwinders. For decades, while uranium miners and those affected by Nevada's nuclear tests received federal compensation, the residents of the Tularosa Basin and surrounding counties—mostly Hispanic and Native American families—were left out of the narrative entirely. They were the forgotten casualties of the Trinity test, the world's first nuclear detonation, which occurred on July 16, 1945, roughly 40 miles west of White Sands Missile Range.

The Documentary's Power

Lipman's documentary, originally premiered in 2023 but re-edited following the RECA expansion, traces the personal and collective journey of the Downwinders. At its emotional center is Tina Cordova, a Latina cancer survivor whose tireless activism became the driving force behind decades-long efforts to bring recognition and compensation to her community. Through her determined quest, the film unravels a troubling historical narrative: communities that were never warned of radioactive danger, who drank contaminated water and milk, who consumed produce and livestock exposed to lethal fallout, and who raised generations of children in the shadow of an invisible death.

The film does not shy away from the broader context of nuclear injustice in the Southwest. It examines not only the Trinity Downwinders but also Native American and Hispanic uranium miners whose sacred lands were scarred by government mining operations. Together, these stories reveal a deliberate pattern of environmental racism—the targeting of vulnerable communities in service of national security and nuclear ambitions, with little regard for the human cost.

Political Leadership Takes a Stand

What distinguished Wednesday's screening was the unmistakable show of political support. Congressman Vasquez, who represents the congressional district encompassing Otero County and the most affected communities, took the stage to affirm his commitment to environmental justice and the health and economic recovery of those harmed by nuclear testing. His presence signaled that the Downwinders' cause has moved from the margins of advocacy to the center of political priorities

But the most potent symbol of validation came from Deb Haaland. As the first Native American to serve as U.S. Interior Secretary—a position with direct historical ties to nuclear testing and indigenous lands—Haaland brought moral authority to the moment. Her appearance at the screening was not merely ceremonial. It represented a federal leadership that understands the intersection of nuclear history, indigenous sovereignty, and environmental justice in a way few others can. Her words of support for the documentary and for the Downwinders' ongoing struggle to secure full recognition and care carried the weight of someone who knows this fight from the inside.

The Q&A session that followed the screening became a direct conversation between community members and two elected officials who pledged to listen and act. This is precisely what the Downwinders have long demanded: not pity, not historical footnotes, but acknowledgment, accountability, and sustained political commitment.

A Victory Marked by Incompleteness

The RECA expansion of July 2025 was a watershed moment—but it remains a partial victory. Compensation and official recognition, while essential, cannot undo generations of illness, cancer, and premature death. Lipman's documentary serves as both a historical record and an ongoing indictment. By bringing it to the Flickinger Center, with full political backing, the community demonstrated that their story is no longer marginal. It is central to New Mexico's identity and to the nation's reckoning with its nuclear past.

The screening was a reminder that documentary filmmaking, when combined with grassroots activism and political will, can transform how communities see themselves and are seen by the world. Haaland and Vasquez's presence on Wednesday was not gratuitous—it was a statement that the Downwinders' struggle for justice has moved from the margins to the mainstream of New Mexico politics.

Essential Viewing

"First We Bombed New Mexico" is essential viewing for anyone seeking to understand the true cost of America's nuclear age. More than that, Wednesday's screening proved that when a community speaks truth, and when leaders listen, real change becomes possible. The Downwinders' long fight for recognition is far from over, but with documentary filmmaking of this caliber and political support now evident, their voices can no longer be silenced.

item.title: In Memory of Bradley (Brad) Lee Shelton
item.description:
Bradley (Brad) Lee Shelton was born November 2, 1939, to Gerald and Marcilee Shelton on their farm near Lineville, Iowa. Brad passed away in Alamogordo, NM on August 7, 2026.

Brad enjoyed a rewarding Iowa farm boy childhood that included roaming 240 acres with his dogs, riding bikes and playing baseball with friends, feeding chickens, hogs and cows, working with tractors in the cornfield, harvesting oats, and putting up hay. He enjoyed school, 4-H, and Clio, Iowa Methodist Youth Fellowship.

The Shelton family moved to Phoenix, AZ in 1956 due to Marcilee’s severe arthritis. Brad worked in Phoenix with his father, running a service station, and learning how to repair cars, deal with customers, and handle business bookkeeping. He graduated with honors from North Phoenix High School in 1958 after winning the Phoenix Teenage Driving Rodeo. Brad made many lifelong friends in the Wesley Fellowship of Garfield Methodist Church. He enrolled in Arizona State University where he became an Air Force ROTC Cadet Officer graduating in 1963 with an Air Force commission and BS in Finance.

Brad became an airplane navigator after pilot training and met his future wife, Carla Sonntag, in Texas and served at bases in AZ, CA, NV, TX, AR, VA, NM, Guam, Thailand, and Japan. He was an instructor navigator and radar navigator in the B-52 and had 184 missions over Southeast Asia during the Vietnam War with awards of nine Air Medals and the Distinguished Flying Cross. He served seven years on combat crews with nuclear alert and had over 4,500 hours in the B-52. He earned an MS in Management from the University of Arkansas in 1974 and became an Accounting Officer retiring from the Air Force as the Budget Officer at Holloman AFB, NM in 1983.

Brad’s next career was as Campus Finance Officer at New Mexico State University-Alamogordo. He was in charge of budgeting, accounting, purchasing, student accounting, bookstore, food services, and maintenance, and served on the administrative council. He was proud of positive financial results thanks to dedicated employees and NMSU-A faculty and staff. He retired from NMSU-A in 2001, but went back twice.

Brad met Martha Curtis at a square dance and they were married January 2, 1994. They enjoyed their Alamogordo home, reading, each other’s families, Grace Methodist Church, square dancing, the mountains, world travel, flying on Southwest Airlines, ocean cruising, and remodeling two houses. In retirement, Brad put his finance degree to use by managing investments, doing volunteer taxes with AARP, and working with NMSU-A Adult Basic Education finances. The Tularosa Basin Historical Society honored Brad with a Lifetime Achievement Award for volunteering his professional knowledge as treasurer, board member, and Form 990 tax preparer. He participated in many church committees, Joy Sunday School Class, and Habitat for Humanity, as well as other mission projects in Mexico and the Southwest U.S. He was a long-time member of the White Sands Rotary Club and honored as a Rotary Paul Harris Fellow, as well as a life member of Military Officers Association of America.

Brad is proud of his three children, all with advanced degrees. He is survived by his dear wife Martha; children, Marilee Shelton-Davenport (Matthew) of Silver Spring, MD, Steven Shelton (Becky) of Holly Springs, NC, Douglas Shelton (Naoko) of San Francisco, CA; grandchildren, Noah and Marisa Davenport and Skye, Sage, Ronan, and Una Shelton; sister, Nancy Noble (Bob) of Wintersburg, AZ; Martha’s children, Toby Smith (Chad) of Ruidoso, NM and Lari Reddell (Adam) of Smithville, TX; Martha’s grandchildren, Whitney Ames (Ryan) of Las Cruces, NM, Averi Franco (Prince) of Fort Worth, TX, Brent and Cameron Reddell of Smithville, TX; great grandchildren, Andrew, Baylee, and Aaron Franco.

Brad is predeceased by his stillborn son, Lawrence; his parents; and his brother, Stanley.

A Graveside Service will be held at 1:00 pm on Saturday, August 15, 2026, at Monte Vista Cemetery with Military Honors. A Memorial Service will follow at 2:00 pm at Grace United Methodist Church.

In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Grace Methodist Church.

item.title: In Memory of James Matthew Lyons

He is also survived by his brothers, Edward Lyons and Robert Lyons; his sisters, Carol Lyons, Melanie Hallbeck, and Tyana Lehman; his former wives, Yolanda Mendez and Melinda Vecellio. Most of all, James will be remembered for the love he had for his family, his unforgettable sense of humor, his willingness to help others, and the lasting impression he made on everyone fortunate enough to know him. item.title: Tularosa Unites to Overcome Water Crisis, Eyes Future Infrastructure - A Conversation with Mayor Cooksey
item.description:
Tularosa, New Mexico, faced a critical test of community resolve this week when heavy mountain rains sent debris cascading into the village’s primary water intake pipe, threatening to exhaust the region’s already-limited reserves. But swift action by local utility workers, combined with an outpouring of support from local businesses, regional institutions, and neighboring tribes, averted disaster in a display of the kind of cooperation that keeps small rural communities functioning.

“This was a real crisis situation,” said Mayor Debbie Cooksey. “But what we saw was the best of our community stepping up when we needed them most.”

Hear the complete interview and conversation between the Mayor of Tularosa and Alamogordo Town News Streaming Journalist Anthony Lucero on KALHRadio.org via the link below…

Crisis Strikes

The problem emerged when debris from burn scars upstream clogged the intake pipe drawing water from the creek—Tularosa’s sole water source. With reserves plummeting and the village facing a potential complete water shutdown, Utility Manager Angel Morback and his team sprang into action, rapidly diagnosing the blockage and beginning cleanup operations.

“Our utility team worked around the clock to resolve this,” Cooksey said. “Angel Morback’s expertise and dedication made all the difference.”

While repairs were underway, emergency water trucks sustained residents as the village’s supplies dwindled. What came next, however, underscored the strength of Tularosa’s institutional relationships.

Community Rallies

Donations poured in from an unlikely coalition of supporters. Local retailers including Lowe’s, Home Depot, Albertsons, and Walmart contributed water supplies. More significantly, Holloman Air Force Base—a major presence in the region—and the Muscalero Apache Nation provided substantial emergency assistance.

“The hospital, the military base, tribal leadership—everyone recognized this was an emergency and acted accordingly,” Cooksey said. “That kind of cooperation doesn’t happen everywhere.”

Within days, the utility team had cleared the blockage and restored water flow. Though a boil water advisory was issued as a precautionary measure while water systems were being combined, multiple tests quickly confirmed the safety of the village’s water supply. The advisory was lifted shortly thereafter.

Looking Forward

The crisis, while resolved quickly, has reinforced long-standing concerns about the village’s vulnerability. Tularosa depends entirely on a single water source—a risky proposition in a desert environment where natural disasters, debris flows, and potential spills could again threaten supply.

“Securing a second water source has been a priority for years,” Cooksey explained. “We have a well that exists, but we need extensive new piping to connect it to our tanks. It’s a significant infrastructure project, but it’s essential for long-term resilience.”

In the meantime, the village continues pursuing other community improvements. A planned splash pad project faces delays due to evolving state environmental and safety requirements, though Cooksey expressed confidence in completing it within her current term.

“These regulations change, and we have to adapt,” she said. “But it’s worth it to provide amenities our community deserves.”

A Model of Governance

What struck observers most, perhaps, was not just the crisis response but the apparent unity of local leadership throughout. Cooksey spoke pointedly about the contrast between Tularosa’s cohesive governing board and the dysfunction plaguing some neighboring municipalities and other water and sanitation districts. 

“We have a board that works together,” she said. “When we face challenges, we face them as a team. That makes all the difference in what we can accomplish.”

As Tularosa moves forward, the water crisis appears to have crystallized what residents already knew: a small rural community’s greatest asset isn’t infrastructure or resources, but the willingness of neighbors, institutions, and leaders to work toward common goals.

“We learned something important this week,” Cooksey reflected. “We learned that when things get tough, Tularosa doesn’t just survive—we thrive.”

item.title: Join for Fiesta of Hope 2026—A Night of Color, Music, and Purpose
item.description:
Alamogordo nonprofit marks third year of signature fundraiser, expanding critical services for abuse survivors

When a child in Otero or Lincoln County experiences abuse, neglect, or witnesses violence, there’s one place designed specifically to help them—and one place only. Kid’s Inc. Child Advocacy Center, headquartered on Cuba Avenue in Alamogordo, is the sole child advocacy center serving both counties and one of just 11 across all of New Mexico.

This August 22, the organization is hosting its third annual Fiesta of Hope gala, a celebration that underscores both the vibrancy of the community and the serious work happening behind the scenes. The event at The Tea Shed represents far more than an evening of catered dinner and dancing—every dollar raised directly funds comprehensive services that would otherwise leave some of the region’s most vulnerable children without support.

A Multidisciplinary Response to a Difficult Reality

Kid’s Inc. operates through what professionals call a Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) approach, coordinating law enforcement, child protective services, medical professionals, mental health providers, and victim advocates to respond to cases of child abuse in a unified, trauma-informed way.

The center’s services include forensic interviewing—structured conversations with children conducted in a specially designed, child-friendly environment by trained professionals—along with family advocacy, crisis counseling, and connections to medical and mental health care. The organization also provides community education and works on legislative advocacy to strengthen child protection laws across the state.

In recent years, Kid’s Inc. has even welcomed Sunny, a courthouse facility dog trained to provide emotional support to children during forensic interviews and throughout the legal process. Sunny’s presence alone has proven to reduce anxiety and help traumatized children open up about their experiences.

“Every ticket, every bid, every dollar goes straight to supporting children and families who are healing from abuse, neglect, and violence,” the organization emphasized in its fundraising materials. For a region where child advocacy resources are stretched thin, that direct impact matters enormously.

Building Community Support

The Fiesta of Hope has grown into a signature Alamogordo event precisely because it tackles a sobering issue while maintaining the spirit of celebration and hope. This year’s theme—“Community. Compassion. Collaboration. Champions”—reflects the organization’s belief that child protection requires the entire community’s involvement.

Attendees can expect a full evening: a catered dinner, full cash bar with signature cocktails, live DJ and dance floor, and a silent auction featuring one-of-a-kind items and experiences. Guests are encouraged to wear fiesta attire or their favorite eveningwear.

Tickets are $65 per person or $100 for two. Those interested in making a larger impact can become event sponsors. All proceeds benefit Kid’s Inc.’s direct services to children and non-offending caregivers navigating the aftermath of trauma.

For tickets or to inquire about sponsorship opportunities, visit kidsinccac.com or call 575-214-2558.

item.title: Commissioners Unanimously Approve Liquor License Renewal for Cottonwood Canyon Winery
item.description:
Longtime Family Vineyard Continues Its Legacy with Full Local Support

At a public hearing held earlier this week, county commissioners unanimously approved the renewal of the liquor license for Cottonwood Canyon Winery, a family-owned vineyard with nearly five decades of deep roots in the community.

The meeting, which opened with a prayer and pledge of allegiance, featured a single agenda item dedicated to the winery’s license renewal. The applicant presented the vineyard’s storied history, tracing the family’s connection to the property back to 1976—when what was then a personal dream became a lasting commitment to the land.

A Legacy of Stewardship

Cottonwood Canyon Winery represents more than a commercial enterprise; it stands as a testament to intergenerational dedication and family continuity. The applicant emphasized how the business carries forward a vision that has shaped the property and community for generations, underscoring the emotional and cultural significance of the operation beyond its economic value.

The winery’s presence is further enriched by historical vineyard paintings that adorn the property, connecting the family business to the region’s cultural heritage and local identity.

Streamlined Approval Process

The licensing hearing proceeded without public opposition. No comments were submitted during the public comment period, suggesting broad community acceptance of the renewal. This absence of objections—combined with the winery’s proven track record of regulatory compliance—facilitated a straightforward approval process.

Commissioner statements reflected strong appreciation for the family’s longstanding stewardship of the property and recognition of the positive community impact the winery has generated over decades of operation.

Unanimous Support Signals Confidence

The unanimous vote by commissioners demonstrates solid institutional backing for the business, affirming both the winery’s regulatory standing and its valued place in the local landscape. The renewal of an existing license—rather than approval of a new application—indicates that Cottonwood Canyon Winery has consistently met regulatory requirements and maintained responsible operations under local oversight.

For the family and the broader community, the decision represents continued validation of their commitment to preserving local heritage while contributing to the region’s economic and cultural vitality.

item.title: Alexander Wilson Arrested on Sexual Exploitation of Children Charges
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, NM — The Criminal Investigations Division has arrested Alexander Wilson, 26, a resident of Alamogordo, following an extensive investigation into the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

The investigation began on April 15, 2026, when the Criminal Investigations Division received a cyber tip from the New Mexico Department of Justice. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) had detected that an Alamogordo resident was uploading suspected CSAM to a cloud service.

Swift Identification and Search

Investigators quickly identified the suspect as Wilson. Following the identification, law enforcement obtained a search warrant for Wilson’s residence. During the execution of the warrant, authorities seized a cell phone and multiple computers belonging to the suspect.

Forensic examinations conducted by the Criminal Investigations Division’s Digital Forensics team revealed hundreds of images and videos consistent with CSAM on the seized devices.

Charges Filed

After several months of comprehensive digital evidence examination, investigators applied for an arrest warrant through Otero County Magistrate Court. On August 13, 2026, Wilson was taken into custody and transported to the Otero County Detention Center.

Wilson has been charged with:

• One Count of Sexual Exploitation of Children (Possession, Under 13)

Multi-Agency Task Force

This case was handled as part of the New Mexico Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, which works to locate, track, and apprehend internet child predators and child pornographers throughout New Mexico. The task force comprises over 90 federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies and receives funding through an Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention (OJJDP) grant administered by the New Mexico Department of Justice.

Report Suspected Child Exploitation

Anyone with information about suspected child predators is urged to contact local or federal law enforcement. Anonymous reports can also be made through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children at:

• Website: http://www.missingkids.org/cybertipline

• Phone: 1-800-THE-LOST (1-800-843-5678)

item.title: Aug 14th thru 17th, 2026 MANDATORY BOIL WATER ADVISORY ISSUED FOR TIMBERON WATER DISTRICT
item.description:
August 14, 2026 — Timberon NM

The Timberon Water and Sanitation District has issued a mandatory boil water advisory effective immediately after E. Coli bacteria were confirmed in the water supply during routine testing on Wednesday. This mandatory directive follows weeks of precautionary boil advisories issued throughout July and represents an escalation in water quality concerns affecting residents of the district.

"This is a serious matter that requires immediate action from all residents," said a spokesperson for the Timberon Water and Sanitation District. "We are taking every step necessary to resolve this situation and restore safe drinking water as quickly as possible."

WHAT RESIDENTS NEED TO KNOW

The E. Coli bacteria were discovered during special water samples collected on August 14, 2026, in connection with routine line repair operations. This latest development marks a significant escalation from the precautionary boil advisories that were in effect multiple times during July.

Effective immediately, all residents served by the Timberton Water and Sanitation District must:

● Boil all water for at least three minutes before drinking or allow it to cool● Use bottled water as an alternative to boiled water● Use boiled or bottled water for brushing teeth, making ice, washing dishes, and preparing food

Continue these precautions until further notice from the water district.

HEALTH RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH E. COLI CONTAMINATION

E. Coli bacteria indicate that water may be contaminated with human or animal waste. Consumption of contaminated water can cause serious gastrointestinal illness in individuals of all ages, though certain populations face heightened risk.

Symptoms of E. Coli contamination include:

● Severe diarrhea and abdominal cramps● Nausea and vomiting● Headaches● Fever in some cases

VULNERABLE POPULATIONS AT GREATER RISK

Health officials urge special caution for infants, young children, elderly individuals, and anyone with compromised immune systems. These populations should consult with their healthcare providers regarding the use of tap water and should prioritize bottled water consumption during this advisory.

Anyone experiencing symptoms consistent with E. Coli infection should seek medical attention immediately.

CONTEXT: JULY PRECAUTIONARY ADVISORIES

The current mandatory advisory comes after a series of precautionary boil water notices were issued multiple times throughout July. Those precautionary measures were implemented as a safeguard when water quality testing indicated potential vulnerability to contamination during routine maintenance operations.

While those July advisories were later lifted as precautionary measures, the detection of E. Coli bacteria this week has now prompted the escalation to a mandatory boil water advisory.

This distinction is critical—a mandatory advisory indicates confirmed contamination and requires immediate compliance by all residents.

WATER DISTRICT RESPONSE AND TIMELINE FOR RESOLUTION

Water System Operations Personnel from the Timberton Water and Sanitation District are actively working  to disinfect all affected areas within the distribution system. The water district has established an aggressive timeline for resolving the contamination.

According to district officials, they anticipate bringing water quality back to safe standards on or before August 17, 2026. Once bacterial testing confirms the elimination of E. Coli throughout the system, residents will receive notification that the boil water advisory has been lifted.

IMPORTANT CONTACT INFORMATION

For questions or additional information regarding the boil water advisory, residents should contact the Timberton Water and Sanitation District:

Wendy Case: (903) 327-6624

Alex Salas: (575) 932-8356

Residents are urged to share this information with neighbors, schools, businesses, nursing homes, and other community members who may not have received direct notification from the water district.

This is an ongoing situation, and updates will be provided as more information becomes available. Residents should regularly check the Alamogordo Town News website and local news outlets for the latest information and directly with staff of the TWSD.

item.title: WALMART RECALLS TOMATO BISQUE SOUP KITS OVER POTENTIAL ALLERGEN CONTAMINATION
item.description:
August 15, 2026 — Walmart has announced a voluntary recall of select batches of its Great Value Tomato Bisque Soup Kits due to the potential presence of undeclared milk allergens, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) confirmed today.

The affected soup kits, sold under the Great Value brand nationwide, may contain milk ingredients not identified on the product label, posing a serious risk to consumers with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

Product Details

The recalled products include:

• Product: Great Value Tomato Bisque Soup Kit

• Package Size: 20 oz boxes

• UPC Codes: 0-78742-51683-2 and 0-78742-51684-9

• Production Dates: June 1 – July 15, 2026

• Affected Stores: Walmart locations nationwide to include New Mexico 

What Customers Should Do

Walmart is urging consumers who purchased the affected products to:

1. Stop consuming the product immediately

2. Return unopened boxes to any Walmart store for a full refund, no receipt required

3. Discard any opened packages

4. Contact the Walmart customer service hotline at 1-800-WALMART with questions

Consumers who have experienced allergic reactions after consuming the product are encouraged to consult their healthcare provider.

FDA Investigation

The FDA was notified of the recall after a consumer complaint reported milk residue in a product that carried no allergen warning. The agency has confirmed that investigation is ongoing to determine the source of the contamination in the manufacturing process.

“Consumer safety is our top priority,” said Dr. Margaret Chen, FDA Division Director for Food Safety. “We are working closely with Walmart and their suppliers to prevent similar incidents and ensure all affected products are removed from shelves.”

Company Statement

A Walmart spokesperson released the following statement: “We take food safety extremely seriously. We immediately launched an investigation when we learned of this issue and have initiated this voluntary recall out of an abundance of caution. We are working with our supplier and the FDA to identify how this contamination occurred and to implement corrective measures.”

The company estimates approximately 47,000 units have been distributed nationwide through its retail locations and online grocery delivery services.

No Injuries Reported

As of August 15, 2026, Walmart and the FDA report no confirmed illnesses or injuries related to the recalled products.

Product Impact

This is the latest in a series of food safety recalls this year. Great Value, Walmart’s in-house brand, has faced two other recalls in 2026—one involving frozen vegetables and another concerning canned beans.

Consumers may also contact the Walmart Recall Hotline at 1-877-WALMART or visit www.walmart.com/recalls for additional product information and updates.

item.title: New Mexico State Police Ends Dangerous Multi-Agency Pursuit with Successful PIT Maneuver
item.description:
Lea County — August 12, 2026 — New Mexico State Police (NMSP) assisted the Lea County Sheriff’s Office in bringing a high-speed pursuit to a safe conclusion after a driver engaged in a series of reckless and dangerous maneuvers that endangered both law enforcement and the public.

The Initial Stop Attempt

The incident began when Lea County Sheriff’s deputies attempted to stop a vehicle for driving recklessly through a school zone and nearly striking another vehicle. When signaled to pull over, the driver immediately fled the scene.

Escalating Danger

What followed was an escalating display of dangerous driving behavior. The fleeing driver traveled at speeds reaching approximately 105 miles per hour and at one point drove westbound in the eastbound lanes of Highway 82, creating an imminent collision hazard for oncoming traffic.

As the pursuit continued onto Highway 457, the driver’s erratic behavior intensified. The driver repeatedly left the roadway, executed multiple U-turns, and came dangerously close to striking oncoming vehicles. During an attempt by officers to deploy stop sticks, the driver allegedly maneuvered the vehicle directly toward a Lea County Sheriff’s deputy before swerving around him at the last moment.

Safe Resolution

An NMSP officer skillfully executed a Precision Intervention Technique (PIT) maneuver, successfully disabling the vehicle and bringing the pursuit to an end. The driver was immediately taken into custody.

Arrest and Charges

The driver, identified as 25-year-old Christina Clayton, was arrested at the scene. Officers observed signs consistent with possible impairment. Clayton has been charged with:

• Speeding

• Reckless Driving

• Aggravated Assault Upon a Peace Officer with a Deadly Weapon

• Two counts of Aggravated Fleeing a Law Enforcement Officer

No Injuries Reported

Despite the dangerous nature of the pursuit and the high speeds involved, no officers or members of the public sustained injuries during the incident.

The New Mexico State Police commended the collaborative efforts of all agencies involved in safely concluding this high-risk situation and protecting the public during a volatile incident.

item.title: Silver Edges Alamogordo in Defensive Battle at Silver City Tournament Friday Evening
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. Alamogordo High School’s boys soccer team suffered a heartbreaking 2-1 defeat to Silver on Saturday in the opening match of the Silver City Round Robin Tournament at Ben Altimirano Soccer Complex.

The match remained scoreless through the first half, with both teams locked in a defensive struggle. The Tigers broke through in the 42nd minute to take a 1-0 lead, but Silver answered back quickly after the intermission, equalizing in the 49th minute on a goal by Kyle Tamayo.

The shift in momentum proved costly for Alamogordo. Silver capitalized on the Tigers’ defensive lapses to score the match-winner and secure the 2-1 victory.

“It’s a tough loss in a tournament setting,” said Tigers head coach following the match. “We had our chances, and we competed hard, but we need to tighten up our defense and convert our opportunities.”

Tamayo’s goal kept the Tigers competitive throughout the second half, but Alamogordo couldn’t find the equalizer despite sustained pressure late in the match.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 0-1 in tournament play. The Tigers will look to bounce back quickly when they face Miyamura later today at 12:30 PM, seeking their first win of the tournament.

The Silver City Round Robin Tournament continues Saturday at Ben Altimirano Soccer Complex reported by Journalist Chris Edwards.

item.title: In Memory of Beth Broughton
item.description:
The spirit of our beloved Connie Beth Broughton returned home to her Heavenly Father on August 1, 2026, at the age of 66. She passed away peacefully at her home in Alamogordo, in the presence of her husband, daughter and son.

Connie was born on April 14, 1960, in Saint George, Utah. She was the sixth and last child of Charles Victor Anderson and Beth (Andrus) Anderson. She is survived by her loving husband of almost 40 years, Collin Broughton, daughter Darla Broughton, son Reece Broughton, brother Dennis (Peggy), brother Craig (Laura), sister Karla Clark (Richard), and brother Brent (Brooke). She is preceded in death by her parents and a brother Steven.

Connie’s first love was music, and she looked for ways to be involved with music throughout her life. She learned to play the piano in her youth then added the flute and piccolo in junior high and high school. She was accomplished enough at the piano in her mid-teens to play hymns for church services. Later in life she learned to play instruments such as the harp, accordion, steel drums and ukulele. She shared her musical talents throughout her life in various ways: as the pianist for Community of Christ Church, as the organist for St. John’s Episcopal Church, and playing preludes and concerts at Grace Methodist Church and a Christmas concert at Bethel Baptist Church. She also accompanied her children’s orchestra class performances on the snare drum and other percussion instruments. She taught both her children how to read music and play the piano, and after they were grown and moved away from home, she started teaching piano lessons as another way to extend her love of music to others.

For family summer trips while Connie was growing up, they traveled in a van which her father had customized with a double bunk bed in place of the rear bench seat. Family trips included the Arches, Dinosaur National Monument, Yellowstone, Hole in the Rock and many others.

Connie was always at the top of her academic class. She had to work hard at times to maintain her A’s, but she really wanted to excel and succeed in her studies. She was always on the honor roll at school, and was one of the top students of her graduating high school class. Connie graduated from Dixie High School in Saint George UT. She received her degree of associate in science from Dixie College (now Southern Utah University). She also attended Utah State University.

After graduating from high school, Connie worked at Bryce Canyon National Park for the summer. It became one of her favorite places on earth and was one of the places she and Collin visited on their honeymoon.

During 1981-1982 Connie served a full-time mission for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in the England London East Mission.

Connie was introduced to Collin by a mutual friend, sometime during the summer of 1985. They started dating in the spring of 1986 and got engaged in early August of that year. They were married in the Saint George Utah temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on October 10, 1986.

Connie was a devoted mother to her two children and was intimately involved as a homeschool mom from the start of their education through high school. It brought her great satisfaction to watch her children learn and grow in knowledge, and she very much enjoyed learning along with them. She participated in local homeschool groups with her children and made many friends among homeschooling families. She and her family traveled to and camped at many of the national and state parks in New Mexico as part of the history and geography curriculum for her children.

She so much enjoyed being out in nature and was an avid hiker. She kept a record of the over 150 trails that she had hiked within the Sacramento Mountains. She and Collin began hiking together even before they were married. A most memorable hike was a 6-hour climb to the top of Mt. Nebo in Utah, where Collin proposed marriage to Connie.

From the time Connie was very young, each year the Anderson family would get together to celebrate Grandma Anderson’s birthday. That birthday celebration eventually turned into a regular family reunion where Connie enjoyed playing with her cousins and visiting with members of the Anderson family.
After she and Collin retired, they bought a motorhome and joined the Family RV Association. They enjoyed participating in the conventions and rallies organized by FRVA and made many new friends.

A life celebration will be held on Saturday, August 22, 2026, between 2 and 4 pm at The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, 1800 23rd St, Alamogordo NM. Family and friends are warmly invited for a time of fellowship and light refreshments as they share memories and celebrate Connie’s remarkable life.

Please arrange for any flowers to be delivered to 3100 Los Robles, Alamogordo, NM 88310.

item.title: Lady Alamogordo Tigers Soccer Split Games at Silver City Tournament
item.description:
Silver N.M.- The Alamogordo Lady Tigers had a mixed performance at the Silver City Tournament this weekend, securing a victory in their opening match before falling to Miyamura in a contest cut short by severe weather.

First Match Victory

Alamogordo dominated their opening matchup against Silver, claiming a 2-1 victory behind goals from London Curry and Zoey Spataro. Curry struck first to put the Lady Tigers ahead 1-0 at the 50-minute mark, with Spataro adding an insurance goal to seal the win.

item.title: Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range Reports Strong July Performance; Second 100-Yard Bay Operational
item.description:
La Luz, New Mexico Reporting by Journalist Chris Edwards — The Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range is marking a significant expansion with the completion of its second 100-yard multipurpose bay and announcing preparations for two major regional championships in the coming weeks.

Facility Expansion Supports Growing Demand

The newly operational 100-yard bay represents a major capacity upgrade. Clean fill material has been delivered and spread across the impact berm and 40 feet along side berms, thanks to donations from local nonprofit organizations. The facility’s decision to construct 100-yard deep bays is already proving beneficial, providing ideal depths for diverse shooting events.

“This depth is ideal for so many different shooting events,” said Mark Douglas, Range Director.

Strong July Operations

The range safely served 816 people in July, including 69 participants in five competitions and events. This month’s activity reflects the facility’s growing importance as a regional shooting venue.

The range continues to support 10 different law enforcement agencies, including the Alamogordo Police Department, Otero County Sheriff’s Department, New Mexico State Police, U.S. Border Patrol, U.S. Air Force Office of Special Investigations, and several others.

Regional Championships Bring National Attention

This weekend, the USPSA Area 2 Steel Challenge Championship will draw competitors from Florida to California. Often described as “drag racing with a gun,” the event will utilize all eight General-Purpose bays. The 200-yard bay is being used for participant parking, while the 50-yard bay serves as a function test area. The Otero Practical Shooting Association is hosting and coordinating the competition.

Looking ahead, the range will host the USPSA Area 2 High Desert NM Sectional Championship during the third week of October. The event has already generated significant interest, with 250 registered participants and a waiting list. The new multipurpose bay was one of the key factors in bringing this prestigious championship back to the Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range.

Financial and Operational Update

July brought $7,738.87 in income from fees, target and snack sales, donations, passes, and taxes. The facility’s diverse revenue streams reflect its multi-purpose mission serving competitive shooters, law enforcement agencies, and recreational users.

In July, the range sold 57 passes of various categories, with notable demand from military discount holders (32 passes) and families seeking recreational access.

Community Connections

The report highlighted two touching moments. Staff discovered an abandoned briefcase at the front gate, which turned out to be a donation from a longtime customer who passed away in 2025—a high-quality metallic rifle rest that will serve future range users.

The facility also hosted some unexpected summer visitors: four baby skunks that took refuge under the classroom deck, obtaining water from the HVAC condensation line. The skunks behaved considerately, moving out within a few weeks.

Facility Improvements Continue

The range recently replaced two 25-year-old signs along South Scenic Drive, which serves as a popular walking and exercise area. The facility also coordinated mileage markers along Scenic Boulevard with the Friends of the Land and Legacy Recreation (FOLLR) organization, promoting both the shooting range and the outdoor recreation area.

Growing Digital Presence

The range’s online visibility continues expanding. Facebook generated 7,256 views in July, representing a 57 percent increase from July 2025. Google Business Profile interactions reached 41 calls (up 5.1% year-over-year), with 128 direction requests. Searches for “shooting range” and “shooting range near me” continue to drive discovery of the facility.

item.title: PNM BILLING CRISIS DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - In what could be the most significant consumer protection crisis facing Alamogordo families in recent memory, Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) continues to impose unexplained billing increases of $100 to $300 per month on residents already struggling with the rising cost of living.

What makes the situation worse: some residents report bills showing usage three times higher than normal—a discrepancy PNM blames on short-staffed meter readers and estimated billing rather than actual usage readings.

Only one local political leader has publicly challenged these practices: Mayor Sharon McDonald, who directly contacted PNM leadership to express municipal concerns about the billing abuse.

Estimated Billing: The Hidden Problem

Dozens of Alamogordo residents report the same troubling pattern: their PNM electricity bills have skyrocketed due to estimated billing rather than actual meter readings.

"I'm an elderly woman on a fixed income," one affected resident shared. "My PNM bill jumped $280 one month. I didn't add any new appliances. I didn't change my usage. When I called PNM to ask why, they couldn't give me a straight answer other than that they're short-staffed in meter readers and may have estimated my usage."

This is the core of the problem: PNM is charging residents based on estimated usage rather than actual meter readings, and when residents call to verify the charges, they receive vague explanations about staffing shortages instead of concrete explanations or corrections.

Families are forced to choose between paying utility bills and purchasing groceries. Elderly residents on fixed incomes face the choice between staying cool in Alamogordo's summer heat and maintaining other basic necessities.

Mayor McDonald Takes Action

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald has contacted PNM leadership directly to express the city's concerns regarding the systematic billing problems affecting residents. She made clear that these are not isolated customer service complaints—they represent a widespread pattern demanding corporate accountability.

"This is exactly what we should expect from elected leadership," consumer advocate and District 51 candidate Grace Nagamine said. "Mayor McDonald recognized that Alamogordo's families needed someone with a voice loud enough to reach corporate headquarters. She answered that call.

The question now is: where are the others?"

Nagamine Provides Action Plan for Residents

District 51  NM State Representative candidate Grace Nagamine has issued a comprehensive action plan providing Alamogordo residents with direct pathways to hold PNM accountable through official regulatory channels.

"This isn't about social media posts," Nagamine emphasized. "This is about making noise where it actually counts—with regulators and corporate leadership who have legal obligations to respond."

Residents can take action immediately:

FILE A COMPLAINT with the Public Regulation Commission at:

https://www.prc.nm.gov/consumer-relations/file-a-complaint/

Phone: (505) 827-4500 

SUBMIT A COMPLAINT to the New Mexico Attorney General at:

https://nmdoj.gov/get-help/submit-a-complaint/

Phone: (505) 827-6000 | Email: consumer@nmag.gov

SEND A CERTIFIED LETTER to PNM Corporate Headquarters:

One First Financial Center, Albuquerque, NM 87158

CALL PNM PUBLIC RELATIONS to formally document your complaint:

(505) 241-2700 (Business Hours, Monday-Friday)

The Silence from Other Political Leaders

As families face $100-$300 monthly billing increases from estimated usage, most of Alamogordo's political establishment has remained silent. City commissioners, county commissioners, and state representatives have offered no public statements, contacted no PNM leadership, and requested no regulatory investigations to date via any public statements. 

This is not a complex issue requiring expert analysis. Alamogordo families are being overcharged based on estimated usage. They cannot get explanations. They are suffering financial hardship.

Why Official Complaints Matter

The power to demand accountability rests with citizens, not political figures. Formal complaints to the Public Regulation Commission carry legal weight. Complaints to the Attorney General create an official record. Certified letters to corporate headquarters require documented response.

Social media posts change nothing. Official complaints to regulatory agencies change everything.

If enough residents file formal complaints, the Public Regulation Commission will be forced to investigate. If systematic overbilling is confirmed, PNM will face enforcement actions, penalties, and demands for customer remediation.

ACT NOW

Document your bills and usage patterns

File a complaint with the PRC online or by phone

Submit a complaint to the Attorney General's office

Send a certified letter to PNM Corporate demanding explanation

Call PNM Public Relations to formally document your complaint

Do not accept vague explanations. Do not allow PNM to hide behind customer service scripts. Make noise where it counts.

item.title: Tularosa Water Tank Reaches 22 Feet as Village Urges Continued Conservation Efforts
item.description:
Tularosa residents have made meaningful progress in the ongoing water crisis, with the village’s main water tank now reaching 22 feet, according to an update released this week. However, officials are cautioning against complacency, warning that overall water usage has begun to increase again despite active water restrictions.

The Village of Tularosa remains under mandatory water conservation measures, which prohibit all outdoor watering and restrict indoor use to essential activities only. While the rising tank level represents weeks of collective conservation efforts by the community, village personnel emphasized that more work remains before restrictions can be safely lifted.

“We have made some really good progress over the last several days, but it appears that our overall water usage is beginning to increase again,” the village stated in this week’s public notice. “We need everyone to keep conserving so we can continue building our levels and get closer to lifting these restrictions.”

Conservation Efforts Showing Results—But Usage Rising

The dual message—celebrating progress while warning of slipping discipline—suggests that some residents may be relaxing conservation habits as visible improvements appear on the horizon. Village officials attribute the recent uptick in usage to this psychological effect, commonly known as “conservation fatigue.”

To maintain momentum toward unrestricted water access, the village is reminding residents of critical conservation practices:

• Wash only necessary loads of laundry and ensure all loads are full capacity

• Reduce shower duration

• Eliminate unnecessary water use throughout the home and yard

• Continue the outdoor watering ban

“The best way we can get there is by continuing to work together and keeping our usage as low as possible right now,” village officials said.

A Community Working Toward Normalcy

Restrictions have tested the patience of Tularosa residents, particularly those managing yards, trees, and plants during the dry months. The inability to irrigate landscaping has raised concerns about vegetation health and property values. However, officials framed ongoing conservation as the fastest path back to normalcy.

“I know everyone is ready to get back to normal, including being able to water our yards, trees and plants,” the village acknowledged in their statement.

What’s Next

Village personnel did not specify the exact water level needed to safely lift restrictions, but indicated that continued coordination between residents and village staff will be essential. As the tank level creeps toward its target, every conservation decision will count.

Tularosa residents are urged to remain vigilant about water use and to remember that collective action has already yielded visible results. The village expressed gratitude for residents’ cooperation and patience, calling on the community to maintain its conservation commitment in the coming weeks.

“Every gallon we conserve helps our Village personnel get us closer to the levels we need to safely return to normal water use,” officials stated. “We’ve come a long way, but we aren’t quite there yet!”

item.title: TIMBERON PRECAUTIONARY BOIL WATER ADVISORY Continues thru 8-21-26
item.description:
Timberon N.M - BOIL YOUR WATER BEFORE USING -Due to E. Coli detected in special samples during line repairs

BOIL YOUR WATER BEFORE USING

Fecal coliform and E. Coli bacteria were found in the water supply on 8/14/2026. These bacteria can make you sick and are a particular concern for people with weakened immune systems.

Bacterial contamination can occur when increased run-off enters the drinking water source (for example, following heavy rains). It can also happen due to a break in the distribution system (pipes) or a failure in the water treatment process.

What should I do? What does this mean?

• DO NOT DRINK THE WATER WITHOUT BOILING IT FIRST.

Bring all water to a boil, let it boil for three minutes, and let it cool before using, or use bottled water. Boiled or bottled water should be used for drinking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing dishes, and food preparation until further notice. Boiling kills bacteria and other organisms in the water.

• Fecal coliforms and E. Coli are bacteria whose presence indicates that the water may be contaminated with human or animal wastes. Microbes in these wastes can cause diarrhea, cramps, nausea, headaches, or other symptoms. They may pose a special health risk for infants, young children, and people with severely compromised immune systems.

• The symptoms above are not caused only by organisms in drinking water. If you experience any of these symptoms and they persist, you may want to seek medical advice. People at increased risk should seek advice from their health care providers about drinking this water.

What is being done?

TWSD-Water System Operations Personnel conducted disinfection procedures 8/14/26-8/16/26. Microorganism sampling results for these efforts were received 8/17/26 and at this time indicate negative for Total Coliform and Fecal Coliform (E. Coli).

Timberon Water and Sanitation District is extending a boil water advisory to 8/21/26 to allow TWSD-Water System Personnel to continue monitoring the distribution system.

The public will be notified once their study is complete and the advisory has been removed.
